Query (actual filters): SELECT users WHERE email = ? | INSERT users
Why it is written this way: Rejects a duplicate email before hashing the password, so response time does not reveal whether an account exists. First user of a brokerage gets role 'hob' and a new brokerage_id uuid.

Query (actual filters): SELECT users WHERE email = ?
Why it is written this way: Verifies the pbkdf2 hash and mints access + refresh tokens. Inactive accounts are refused here rather than at the first API call.

Query (actual filters): SELECT users WHERE id = claims.user_id
Why it is written this way: Re-checks is_active on every refresh so a deactivated account cannot ride out an 8-hour session. Access tokens live 60 min; without this endpoint an 8h session was impossible.

Query (actual filters): none of its own - returns the row already resolved by the auth dependency
Why it is written this way: Profile echo for clients that did not retain the login payload.

Query (actual filters): no database access
Why it is written this way: Starts Google Calendar OAuth. Unconfigured: no client id is set, so it 500s by design.

Query (actual filters): UPDATE users SET google_refresh_token (encrypted)
Why it is written this way: Stores the encrypted Google refresh token. Untested - the Calendar module is future work.

Query (actual filters): SELECT users WHERE email = ? | SELECT invitations WHERE email = ? AND brokerage_id = ? AND status = 'pending' | UPDATE invitations SET status = 'cancelled' | INSERT invitations
Why it is written this way: The brokerage domain is derived from the inviter's own email, never from the request body, and the role is never trusted from the client. Prior pending invites are cancelled so only one token is ever live. A 60-second cooldown returns 429 to block resend spam. Only the SHA-256 hash of the token is stored.

Query (actual filters): SELECT invitations WHERE token_hash = sha256(token) | UPDATE invitations SET status = 'expired' if past expires_at
Why it is written this way: Shows who invited you and to what role before you type a password. Expiry is settled lazily on read instead of by a scheduled job.

Query (actual filters): SELECT users WHERE email = ? | UPDATE invitations SET status='accepted', accepted_at=? WHERE id = ? AND status='pending' | INSERT users
Why it is written this way: The UPDATE is the atomic claim: it only matches while the row is still pending, so two simultaneous accepts cannot both create an account. The new user inherits brokerage_id and role from the invitation, not from the form.

Query (actual filters): sync_activity: SELECT leads WHERE user_id = ? AND conversation_id IS NOT NULL -> per lead SELECT messages WHERE conversation_id = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 1 -> UPDATE leads SET last_activity_at, dnc | list: SELECT leads WHERE user_id = ? AND (owner_name ILIKE ? OR property_address ILIKE ? OR area ILIKE ?) ORDER BY score DESC, id DESC
Why it is written this way: Last activity and DNC are refreshed from the linked threads before the list is read, so the pool can never show a stale stage. Signal and stage filters run in Python: signals are a packed CSV column and stage is derived, so neither is expressible as a portable SQL predicate. NOTE: unpaginated - returns the whole pool.
Where in the UI: Lead Pool tab: table, filters, facet counts

Query (actual filters): SELECT leads WHERE id = ? AND user_id = ? | SELECT conversations WHERE id = lead.conversation_id | SELECT COUNT(messages) + latest message
Why it is written this way: Ownership is in the WHERE clause, so another broker's lead id returns 404 rather than a permission error that would confirm the row exists. Adds score breakdown and the imported details blob.
Where in the UI: Lead Pool tab: details drawer (right slide-in)

Query (actual filters): reads the staged file and SELECTs nothing except to build counts - deliberately no writes
Why it is written this way: Dry run so the row limit and the column mapping are chosen against real counts instead of a guess. Returns a token; the uploaded file waits on disk 30 min so a 50 MB list is not uploaded twice. Re-runs with a new mapping without re-uploading.
Where in the UI: Lead Pool tab: import dialog (counts, column mapping, sample rows)

Query (actual filters): INSERT leads via bulk_save_objects in batches of 1000
Why it is written this way: One lead per readable row - nothing is matched or merged, so importing the same file twice adds every lead twice. Batched because a vendor list runs to six figures and one flush of that size is far slower. limit caps rows from the top of the file; 0 means all.
Where in the UI: Lead Pool tab: import dialog confirm

Query (actual filters): SELECT leads WHERE user_id = ? AND id IN (...) | per lead SELECT conversations WHERE contact = ? AND user_id = ? | INSERT conversations | INSERT messages (outreach.initial) | UPDATE leads SET conversation_id, last_activity_at
Why it is written this way: The one join between the two halves of the product. Per-lead outcomes are returned instead of failing the batch - forty selected leads should not be lost to one bad phone number. Blocks DNC leads, leads with no phone, no address, or already in a campaign. Capped at 200 per campaign.
Where in the UI: Lead Pool tab: selection bar -> campaign dialog

Query (actual filters): DELETE FROM leads WHERE user_id = ? AND id IN (...) - chunked 500 ids per statement
Why it is written this way: Chunked because an IN clause costs one bind parameter per id and every driver caps those (SQLite historically 999); selecting a whole 4000-lead pool has to work. The linked conversation is deliberately kept - a thread Bobbie opened is a record of contact.
Where in the UI: Lead Pool tab: bulk Remove and the row bin icon

Query (actual filters): SELECT leads WHERE id = ? AND user_id = ? | DELETE that row
Why it is written this way: Superseded by the bulk route; retained for scripts and curl.

Query (actual filters): SELECT conversations WHERE user_id = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC | per row latest message + COUNT(messages)
Why it is written this way: Serialises awaiting_broker_reply = (handled_by='broker' AND last message inbound) so the 'needs your reply' badge is computed once on the server rather than in every client.
Where in the UI: SMS tab: conversation list, polled every 5s

Query (actual filters): SELECT conversations WHERE contact = ? AND user_id = ? | COUNT messages - 409 if the thread already has any | INSERT conversations | INSERT messages
Why it is written this way: An empty thread for the same number is reused rather than duplicated, while a thread with history is protected from a second introduction.

Query (actual filters): same serialiser as the list, for one row, scoped by user_id
Why it is written this way: Single-thread refresh.

Query (actual filters): SELECT conversations WHERE id = ? AND user_id = ? | SELECT messages WHERE conversation_id = ? ORDER BY created_at, id
Why it is written this way: Ownership is re-checked on the parent conversation before any message is read.
Where in the UI: SMS tab: open thread, polled every 5s

Query (actual filters): UPDATE conversations SET handled_by='broker', ai_enabled=0 | INSERT messages event_type='broker.message'
Why it is written this way: Sending is an implicit handover: two voices in one thread is worse than an extra click, so stepping in takes ownership of the conversation.
Where in the UI: SMS tab: composer. Follow-ups tab: the composer that appears once the thread is yours.

Query (actual filters): UPDATE conversations SET handled_by = 'bobbie'|'broker', ai_enabled = 1|0
Why it is written this way: The only way Bobbie resumes a broker-owned thread. process_ai_reply returns early unless handled_by='bobbie', so this column - not the UI - is the guarantee that she stays silent.
Where in the UI: SMS tab: 'Take over' / 'Hand back to Bobbie' pill

Query (actual filters): UPDATE conversations SET name, property_address, ai_enabled (+ handled_by kept in step)
Why it is written this way: Toggling autopilot moves ownership with it so the two columns can never disagree.
Where in the UI: not currently called by the UI

Query (actual filters): DELETE messages WHERE conversation_id = ? | DELETE the conversation
Why it is written this way: Messages are deleted first because there is no ON DELETE CASCADE on the FK. Any lead pointing at the thread is released back to the pool on the next lead-pool read.
Where in the UI: SMS tab: thread header bin icon

Query (actual filters): SELECT start_at, end_at FROM bookings WHERE user_id = ?
Why it is written this way: Free slots are computed by subtracting existing bookings from working hours. Bobbie may offer only these, which is what stops her inventing a time.
Where in the UI: no screen - consumed by Bobbie's scheduling layer

Query (actual filters): SELECT bookings WHERE user_id = ? ORDER BY start_at
Why it is written this way: The broker's confirmed meetings.

Query (actual filters): no SQL - ChromaDB vector store + lexical index, fused with Reciprocal Rank Fusion
Why it is written this way: Bobbie's grounded answers come from the indexed PDF, not from the relational database. Exposed for debugging what she is allowed to cite.

Query (actual filters): no SQL - reports the indexed document, chunk count and embedding provider
Why it is written this way: Confirms which document is live and whether semantic retrieval or the lexical fallback is in use.

Query (actual filters): no SQL - re-extracts the PDF and re-embeds every chunk
Why it is written this way: HOB only, because a full re-embed is expensive.

Query (actual filters): SELECT DISTINCT messages.conversation_id JOIN conversations WHERE user_id = ? AND direction = 'inbound' | SELECT conversations WHERE id IN (...) | SELECT messages WHERE conversation_id IN (...) ORDER BY created_at, id | SELECT leads WHERE user_id = ? AND conversation_id IN (...)
Why it is written this way: Lists only threads carrying at least one inbound message - a lead who never answered belongs in the SMS tab, not here. The messages and lead rows for the whole list are fetched in one query each and grouped in Python rather than per conversation. The waiting reason (reply needed / appointment to confirm / no response for N days) is derived on read, like leads.stage, so it can never drift from the thread. Optional ?state= filters on the recorded decision.
Where in the UI: Follow-ups tab: the triage list, polled every 8s

Query (actual filters): SELECT conversations WHERE id = ? AND user_id = ? | SELECT messages WHERE conversation_id = ? | SELECT leads WHERE user_id = ? AND conversation_id = ?
Why it is written this way: One row, re-serialised after every action so the open panel never shows stale state. Ownership is taken from the JWT, so another brokerage gets a 404 rather than a 403.

Query (actual filters): UPDATE conversations SET followup_state = 'pending'|'accepted'|'declined'
Why it is written this way: Records who owns the outcome of a replied lead. Deliberately does NOT touch handled_by: accepting a lead and taking the conversation off Bobbie are separate decisions, and conflating them would silence her the moment someone accepted.

Query (actual filters): UPDATE conversations SET lead_status (+ dnc_alert, ai_enabled, handled_by when set to dnc)
Why it is written this way: A manual status override, and the one path that does not merge with the classifier: the person reading the thread outranks it in either direction, including downgrades. Setting dnc also stops autopilot and hands the thread over, because an owner marked do-not-contact must never be texted again.
Where in the UI: Follow-ups tab: the status dropdown in the panel header

Query (actual filters): SELECT bookings WHERE user_id = ? AND start_at < ? AND end_at > ? | INSERT bookings | UPDATE conversations SET meeting_booked=1 | INSERT messages event_type='broker.booking'
Why it is written this way: Books by hand from the same availability Bobbie offers, so the two can never double-book: the overlap check runs in the transaction that inserts the row and a collision is a 409. The confirmation SMS names the person who booked, not Bobbie, and is stored as 'broker.booking' so the thread never credits her with a human's booking. It is sent with suppress_auto_reply so she does not answer it, and because the booking is already committed a delivery failure comes back as notified=false with a note rather than failing the request. Refused outright for an owner who has opted out.

Query (actual filters): SELECT conversations WHERE contact = from_number ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 1 | INSERT messages direction='inbound' | UPDATE conversations SET lead_status, dnc_alert
Why it is written this way: The only unauthenticated write path - the Ed25519 signature is verified before anything is read. An unknown number is refused rather than creating an ownerless thread. GAP: the lookup is not scoped by user or brokerage, so if two brokers ever hold the same contact the newest thread silently wins.
Where in the UI: called by Telnyx, not by a screen

Query (actual filters): no database access
Why it is written this way: Liveness probe.

Query (actual filters): no SQL - pings Redis and ChromaDB
Why it is written this way: Liveness for the two non-relational stores.

Query (actual filters): SELECT conversations WHERE user_id = ? | per row SELECT messages
Why it is written this way: DEAD CODE. Predates the SMS workspace and duplicates GET /sms/conversations with weaker serialisation. The frontend never calls it. Recommend deleting.

Query (actual filters): SELECT conversations WHERE id = ? AND user_id = ? | SELECT messages ORDER BY created_at
Why it is written this way: DEAD CODE. Duplicate of the /sms equivalent. Recommend deleting.

Query (actual filters): SELECT conversations WHERE id = ? AND user_id = ? | INSERT messages
Why it is written this way: DEAD CODE. Sends without the handover rule, so it could produce a broker message while Bobbie still owns the thread. Recommend deleting.

Query (actual filters): SELECT conversations WHERE id = ? AND user_id = ? | SELECT messages ORDER BY created_at | INSERT ai_runs
Why it is written this way: DEAD CODE. The only writer of ai_runs, and nothing calls it - which is why that table is empty. Recommend deleting, or wiring ai_runs into the live pipeline as an audit log.
